The estimates of a Statistics Canada table, with their confidence limits

Source: R/indigenous_mental_health.R
scests.Rd

Statistics Canada's tables give each estimate on several rows: the estimate itself (a percent, a rate, a count, a life expectancy), its low and high confidence limits, or its coefficient of variation or standard error, all in one statistics column (Statistics, Characteristics, Statistics (3), ...). This puts them side by side, one row per cell of the table and measure, ready for indgap, ordcmp, stdprev and the rest. Every table reads: one without a statistics column (a census count) gives each value as its own estimate, with no limits.

Usage

scests(x)

Arguments

x

A table read by sctidy, a data frame as downloaded, or a table key.

Value

A data frame, one row per cell and measure: the identifying columns, measure, estimate, lower, upper, cisou and quality; the attribute conflvl is the level of the limits, and unmatched names any limits that could not be matched to one measure.

Details

Each label of the statistics column is read as an estimate or as one of its measures of precision, in every form the tables use:

  • "Low 95% confidence interval";

  • "High 95% confidence interval, age-standardized rate";

  • "Confidence interval lower bound of count";

  • "95% confidence interval (upper limit)";

  • "95% confidence interval lower bound, 2020";

  • "Coefficient of variation for percent";

  • "Standard error".

A limit that names its measure is matched to it (ignoring case and spacing); one that names none, or a name that fits several measures ("potential years of life lost" in a table with a number, a crude rate and an age-standardised rate of them), is matched to the measure with the same unit (UOM) whose estimates it contains in every cell, and left unmatched (said in the attribute unmatched) if no single measure fits. A coefficient of variation \(c\) (in percent) gives log-normal limits \(e \exp(\mp z \sqrt{\log(1 + (c/100)^2)})\), which stay positive however large \(c\) is; a standard error \(s\) the limits \(e \mp z s\); the column cisou says which ("published", "cv" or "se"). Published limits that do not contain their own estimate (it happens: a 100% with limits 85.5 to 98.6 in table 41-10-0012) are kept as published and marked "inconsistent"; every comparison of the family warns and leaves such a row out. A limit is matched to a measure when it fits 95% of the cells. Labels are read in English: use the English-language tables.

Every other column but the metadata (VECTOR, COORDINATE, UOM, ...) identifies the cell, DGUID among them (one place name can name several geographies), with the spaces some labels end in trimmed. The quality flag is the estimate's: an F or x estimate is NA (see sctidy), and so are its limits.

References

Statistics Canada (2023). Self-perceived mental health of First Nations people living off reserve, Metis and Inuit by age group and gender. Table 41-10-0067-01. doi:10.25318/4110006701-eng

See also

sctidy, indgap, ordcmp.

Examples

# the layout of a downloaded table: percent and number of persons, with limits for the
# percent
d <- data.frame(REF_DATE = "2022", GEO = "Canada",
                `Indigenous identity` = rep(c("First Nations", "Metis"), each = 4),
                Statistics = rep(c("Number of persons", "Percent",
                                   "Low 95% confidence interval",
                                   "High 95% confidence interval"), 2),
                UOM = rep(c("Persons", "Percent", "Percent", "Percent"), 2),
                VALUE = c(415000, 47.1, 45.2, 49.0, 320000, 50.3, 48.1, 52.5),
                STATUS = "", check.names = FALSE)
scests(d)
#>   REF_DATE    GEO Indigenous identity           measure estimate lower upper
#> 1     2022 Canada       First Nations Number of persons 415000.0    NA    NA
#> 2     2022 Canada       First Nations           Percent     47.1  45.2  49.0
#> 3     2022 Canada               Metis Number of persons 320000.0    NA    NA
#> 4     2022 Canada               Metis           Percent     50.3  48.1  52.5
#>       cisou quality
#> 1      <NA>      ok
#> 2 published      ok
#> 3      <NA>      ok
#> 4 published      ok
# a rate with its coefficient of variation instead of limits
r <- data.frame(GEO = "Canada",
                Characteristics = c("Rate", "Coefficient of variation for rate"),
                VALUE = c(12.5, 8), STATUS = "")
scests(r)
#>      GEO measure estimate    lower    upper cisou quality
#> 1 Canada    Rate     12.5 10.68864 14.61832    cv      ok
